They Can Unlock the Rest of the Night Sky. Made up of three of summer’s brightest stars, the Summer Triangle is an easy starting point for exploring—and photographing—the Milky Way and beyond. The Milky Way arcs above the walls of a gorge, framed by the three bright stars of the Summer Triangle. BABAK TAFRESHI, National Geographic Image Collection By Stefanie Waldek Published August 20, 2026 Stargazing can feel overwhelming when you don’t know where to begin. But in August, three exceptionally bright stars offer an easy starting point. Vega, Deneb, and Altair form the Summer Triangle, an enormous star pattern that rises high in the evening sky across much of the Northern Hemisphere. Once you find it, the triangle can serve as a guide to nearby constellations, deep-sky objects, and the Milky Way. It is also one of the most photogenic regions of the summer sky in August. Here’s how to find the Summer Triangle—and photograph what surrounds it. How to Find the Summer Triangle The Summer Triangle is not a constellation, but an asterism, or a recognizable pattern of stars. Begin with Vega, one of the brightest stars visible from Earth. In mid-August, observers in the Northern Hemisphere can generally find it high overhead. Deneb appears to one side of Vega, while Altair lies farther away, creating a large, elongated triangle. Here's why it happens and where to look. Venus, the Pleiades star cluster, and the bright star Capella rise in the dawn sky above a tufa formation in California’s Mono Lake. BABAK TAFRESHI, National Geographic Image Collection By Stefanie Waldek Published November 12, 2026 Look low in the northeastern sky on an autumn evening, and you might spot something unusual: a bright star flashing red, green, and blue. That’s Capella, one of the brightest stars in the night sky. But despite appearances, the star isn’t actually changing colors. The dazzling display is an optical effect caused by starlight passing through Earth’s atmosphere. And Capella isn’t the only star that puts on this kind of show. “Stars appear to twinkle or shimmer in the night sky, but this is not an inherent trait of stars,” says Emily Watson, astrophysicist and planetarium supervisor at the U.S. Space & Rocket Center. “As the light from a star passes through different densities and temperatures within our atmosphere, the light bends in a process called refraction.” The color flashes happen because Earth’s atmosphere bends different wavelengths of light by different degrees. Two fists thud like anvils onto the wooden tabletop, and the old bones of the Rødbrygga pub shudder in protest. pages.text: Looking for whales—and awe—in Baja California | National Geographic TRAVEL Looking for whales—and awe—in Baja California The Gulf of California was once known as “the aquarium of the world.” But on a recent whale watching trip—and in an era where climate change is making its mark—our writer wonders if it still delivers. The Sea of Cortez is famous for its marine mammals, including fin, minke, humpback whales, seals, and sea lions, as well as common and bottlenose dolphins. Story and video by Kinsey Gidick Published May 15, 2026 When considering a trip to Baja, it’s nearly impossible to dodge the words of two famous men: Jacques Cousteau and John Steinbeck. The pioneering French oceanographer famously called the Gulf of California “the aquarium of the world.” Not surprisingly, that line shows up everywhere—typed into brochures and slipped into itineraries, hovering like a promise. Meanwhile, Steinbeck’s The Log from the Sea of Cortez , the Pulitzer winner’s account of his 1940 six-week, 4,000-mile expedition examining tide pools and collecting specimens along the narrow sea is practically required reading. To be fair, the acclaim is well earned. Steinbeck’s account reads like a dispatch from another, more poetic, planet. But these touchstones sketched a vision of abundance so vivid, especially in a climate-anxious age, that they almost felt like fables: beautiful, sure, yet just distant enough to raise my eyebrow. pages.text: Los Mirlos: Tiny Desk Concert : NPR Accessibility links Skip to main content Keyboard shortcuts for audio player Los Mirlos: Tiny Desk Concert For more than 50 years, Los Mirlos has cultivated its own Peruvian twist on cumbia, featuring reverb-heavy, surf-rock guitar. Los Mirlos: Tiny Desk Concert September 17, 2026 10:00 AM ET Felix Contreras Credit: Photo: Vanessa Castillo/NPR From jazz and Tejano to norteño and ska, 'El Tiny' returns with a takeover from Sept. 15 to Oct. 15 for Latin Music Month . Originally born from Afro-Colombian communities, cumbia spread across the Spanish-speaking world , acquiring distinct musical accents along the way. In Peru, cumbia became particularly popular among oil workers deep in the Amazon. And when Jorge Rodriguez Grández started Los Mirlos in his small hometown of Moyobamba, his band played a regional style called cumbia amazónica, easily identifiable by its electric, reverb-heavy, surf-rock guitar. Sponsor Message Alt.Latino Cumbia: The Musical Backbone Of Latin America Los Mirlos' time behind the Desk is not only a joyful celebration of this music but also a trail of small towns and cities throughout the Amazon jungle. Throughout their performance, these cultural ambassadors share stories and declare their love for cumbia and their tropical homeland. We are so fortunate to host and share with you a group of true pioneers and innovators who, over 50 years later, still effortlessly pump out cumbia grooves. Los Texmaniacs ' music is a living history lesson. The conjunto sound is driven by the button accordion, a mid-19th century instrument that made its way to the U.S.-Mexico border by way of German, Czech and Polish immigrants. But this music is also just perfect for twirling on the dance floor to songs about true love, heartbreak, folk heroes and reflections on life. Los Texmaniacs band leader and bajo sexto player Max Baca had a long-standing musical partnership with Jimenez — they played the Tiny Desk together in 2012 . pages.text: Los Tigres' Tiny Desk, explained : Alt.Latino : NPR Accessibility links Skip to main content Keyboard shortcuts for audio player Los Tigres' Tiny Desk, explained : Alt.Latino Last week we published a Tiny Desk Concert that ended up being unusual for a few reasons. First of all, it was the final production of our sixth annual El Tiny series. This was a very emotional moment for a lot of reasons. People really love Los Tigres del Norte, to the point that playing their albums feels like sitting with family. And if you’ve seen the introduction I gave the band just before they played at the desk you can see that I wasn’t embarrassed to get emotional when I talked about what the band means to me. That emotional intro led to some changes in our process and format that resulted in a huge response from the audience that went viral. The result was a messy moment behind the scenes here at NPR and more than a little confusion for a lot of you. This week’s episode looks back at last week. First we want to share with you, directly from us, an explanation of what happened. But mostly we want to put the spotlight back on the band and their music because for decades they have been bringing out the kind emotions that got this whole thing started. pages.text: Loss of Dependent Coverage | U.S. Department of Labor Skip to main content Loss of Dependent Coverage If your employer’s plan offers coverage for dependent children, your child can stay on your plan until age 26. Once your child "ages out" the child may be eligible for coverage under his or her own employer’s plan, for special enrollment in Marketplace coverage or may be eligible to purchase temporary extended health coverage for up to 36 months under the Consolidated Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act (COBRA). Generally, COBRA covers group health plans maintained by employers with 20 or more employees. pages.description: In addition to the total eclipse that will cast the ancient city in shadow, new hotels and other experiences offer fresh incentive to visit the sphinxes and temples on the banks of the Nile.
pages.text: Luxor's Temples Will Fall Into Darkness for Six Minutes During the 2027 Eclipse | National Geographic TRAVEL BEST OF THE WORLD In 2027, See Luxor in a New Light In addition to the total eclipse that will cast the ancient city in shadow, new hotels and other experiences offer fresh incentive to visit the sphinxes and temples on the banks of the Nile. In the early morning hours outside Luxor, it is common to see dozens of hot-air balloons carrying visitors above ongoing excavation work near the Hungarian Archeological Mission in Thebes. András Zoltai By Zoey Goto Published October 20, 2026 The six-minute “eclipse of the century” in August 2027 will bring an influx of astrotourists to Luxor, but the city has far more to offer than any single celestial event. Straddling both banks of the Nile, Egypt's ancient capital is entering a new chapter, with a host of high-profile openings and experiences to complement its Pharaonic wonders. The lavishly restored Mandarin Oriental Winter Palace and the new Four Seasons Hotel Luxor are both set to welcome guests next year. Also making its debut is the 80-passenger Guardian of the Nile, Egypt's first luxury tourist sleeper train, which will stop in Luxor on its way from Cairo to Aswan. Tour the 3,000-year-old temples of Karnak, then soar above them in a hot-air balloon. Making a Better Battery Credit: Raw Pixel/Pixabay Helping smartphones hold their charge longer. Light-weight and energy-efficient, lithium-ion batteries have long been the battery of choice for powering smartphones, laptops, hoverboards, drones and other portable electronic devices. But even these low-maintenance batteries have their drawbacks—they lose their ability to hold charge after about 3 years, can catch on fire and often have to be recharged daily. To make a better lithium-ion battery or find innovative alternatives, PML researchers in collaboration with scientists from the Material Measurement Laboratory (MML) are studying how lithium batteries behave on some of the tiniest of scales, a few tens of atoms across. The scientists use an instrument that injects with exquisite precision an ultranarrow beam of lithium ions (charged atoms of lithium) into the negative terminal of a laboratory battery. pages.text: Mammals Made By Viruses | National Geographic SCIENCE THE LOOM Mammals Made By Viruses By Carl Zimmer Published February 14, 2012 • 6 min read If not for a virus, none of us would ever be born. In 2000, a team of Boston scientists discovered a peculiar gene in the human genome. It encoded a protein made only by cells in the placenta. They called it syncytin. The cells that made syncytin were located only where the placenta made contact with the uterus. They fuse together to create a single cellular layer, called the syncytiotrophoblast, which is essential to a fetus for drawing nutrients from its mother. The scientists discovered that in order to fuse together, the cells must first make syncytin. What made syncytin peculiar was that it was not a human gene. It bore all the hallmarks of a gene from a virus. Viruses have insinuated themselves into the genome of our ancestors for hundreds of millions of years. They typically have gotten there by infecting eggs or sperm, inserting their own DNA into ours. There are 100,000 known fragments of viruses in the human genome, making up over 8% of our DNA. Most of this virus DNA has been hit by so many mutations that it’s nothing but baggage our species carries along from one generation to the next. Yet there are some viral genes that still make proteins in our bodies. Syncytin appeared to be a hugely important one to our own biology. Originally, syncytin allowed viruses to fuse host cells together so they could spread from one cell to another. Now the protein allowed babies to fuse to their mothers. pages.text: Man with venomous snakes and lizards stopped at German airport Skip to content Site search Home News Sport Business Technology Health Culture Arts Travel Earth Audio Video Live Documentaries Weather Newsletters Watch Live Man with suitcase full of snakes stopped at German airport 15 October 2026 Share Save Add as preferred on Google Paulin Kola German Customs Not all the the snakes and lizards were alive, officials said A man has been stopped at Cologne Bonn Airport in Germany after trying to smuggle in more than 90 lizards and venomous snakes. Customs officials said the 45-year-old Mexican firefighter had looked "conspicuously nervous" as he tried to go through the green - nothing to declare - exit at the airport. They conducted a drugs test on the man - which came back positive for cocaine - before proceeding to check his suitcase. They did not find any drugs, but vipers, rattlesnakes and other species of snakes and lizards, including iguanas, hidden in shampoo and cream bottles, plastic containers and balls of socks. "My colleagues at the airport are used to a lot when it comes to souvenirs in suitcases, but we've never had 37 live venomous snakes and 55 lizards from Mexico before," said Jens Ahland, spokesman for the Cologne Customs office. Some were being kept "in inhumane conditions", Ahland said. Others had died during the journey from Mexico City via Istanbul. The man, who has not been named, told officers that he had brought the animals back as a favour for a Brazilian acquaintance. He was denied entry to Germany and flown back to Istanbul. Search Twitter YouTube Facebook Instagram Flickr LinkedIn Manatee Awareness Month: Protecting Gentle Giants at the Jupiter Inlet Lighthouse Outstanding Natural Area Nov 3, 2026 Every November, Manatee Awareness Month celebrates one of Florida’s most beloved residents: the West Indian manatee. Often called “sea cows” because of their grazing habits, these gentle giants can grow to more than 10 feet long and weigh over 1,000 pounds. Despite their impressive size, manatees are peaceful, slow-moving animals that spend much of their time feeding on aquatic vegetation, resting, and traveling through coastal waters, rivers, estuaries, and springs. West Indian manatees swim in the clear, shallow waters of the Jupiter Inlet Lighthouse Outstanding Natural Area in Jupiter, Florida. The Bureau of Land Management site is the only BLM-managed area where manatees are regularly observed and provides important habitat for these gentle marine mammals. Paula Abreu Pita Manga are Japanese comic books and graphic novels. They are typically written and illustrated by a single person, known as mangaka . Her reports can be heard regularly on NPR's award-winning newsmagazine programs Morning Edition and All Things Considered . Liasson provides extensive coverage of politics and policy from Washington, DC — focusing on the White House and Congress — and also reports on political trends beyond the Beltway. Each election year, Liasson provides key coverage of the candidates and issues in both presidential and congressional races. During her tenure she has covered nine presidential elections — in 1992, 1996, 2000, 2004, 2008, 2012, 2016, 2020, and 2024. Prior to her current assignment, Liasson was NPR's White House correspondent for all eight years of the Clinton administration. She has won the White House Correspondents' Association's Merriman Smith Award for daily news coverage in 1994, 1995, and again in 1997. From 1989-1992 Liasson was NPR's congressional correspondent. Liasson joined NPR in 1985 as a general assignment reporter and newscaster. From September 1988 to June 1989 she took a leave of absence from NPR to attend Columbia University in New York as a recipient of a Knight-Bagehot Fellowship in Economics and Business Journalism. Mario Balotelli heard it all. Perhaps better known for off-field antics than his undeniable - yet arguably wasted - talent with the ball at his feet, the Italian has always attracted headlines. Fifteen years have passed since his famous 'Why always me?' Manchester derby T-shirt celebration, which came just days after a firework was set off in his own bathroom, causing a house fire. The 36-year-old is still playing, now in the United Arab Emirates first division with Al-Ittifaq alongside his biological brother, Enock Barwuah. Here, BBC Sport looks at a career that has included 13 clubs, six countries - and an assist for arguably the most famous goal in Premier League history. Photograph: Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images US military This article is more than 10 months old Mark Kelly sues Hegseth over ‘chilling’ effort to reduce military retirement rank This article is more than 10 months old US defense secretary Pete Hegseth tried to reduce veteran’s pension for speaking out against Trump administration Richard Luscombe Mon 12 Jan 2026 15.14 EST Last modified on Mon 12 Jan 2026 15.22 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Democratic US senator Mark Kelly filed a lawsuit on Monday seeking to nullify the “chilling” attempt by the defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, to reduce the military veteran’s rank and pension as punishment for speaking out against the Trump administration . Hegseth had previously issued a formal censure to Kelly , a decorated retired navy captain and Nasa astronaut, for alleged “seditious statements” he made urging service members to resist unlawful orders . It began a process that could lead to Kelly, a senator for Arizona since 2021, being demoted and having his pension cut. The lawsuit, filed in Washington DC federal court, argues that comments made by Kelly and five other Democratic lawmakers – all military or intelligence veterans – in a short video to service members in November were protected free speech. Marla Morales Marla Morales is the Acting Deputy Assistant Secretary for Spent Fuel and High-Level Waste Disposition. Prior to this role, she was the Director for the Office of Collaboration-Based Siting and Acting Director for the Office of Disposal Research and Development with the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE). Previously, Marla worked for the NRC as a Project Manager working on the environmental analyses for consolidated interim storage facilities, fuel fabrication facilities, independent spent fuel storage installations, uranium recovery activities, and decommissioning facilities. Additionally, Marla led public outreach, government-to-government engagement, and Tribal consultation. Prior to joining the NRC, Marla was a Lead Scientist at SwRI where she began her career working on the Yucca Mountain site assessment. Ms. Morales is a licensed professional geoscientist for the States of Virginia and Texas. She earned a Bachelor of Science degree in Geology from Vanderbilt University and a Master of Science from the University of Texas at San Antonio. Articles by Marla Morales
